title: React routing frameworks data loading server components and deployment
concepts: A production React app needs a routing and rendering architecture that coordinates URL matching, nested layouts, data loading, mutations, pending and error states, asset delivery, and deployment runtime.

Current React guidance recommends starting a whole application with a framework. A framework can support client-only routes, static output, server rendering, streaming, and server features together, without requiring every deployment to use a server.

Next.js App Router uses file-system routes and React Server Components by default for pages and layouts. Client Components add state, event handlers, and browser API access across an explicit client module boundary.

React Router Framework Mode combines Vite, route modules, data loaders and actions, middleware, rendering strategies, and deploy adapters; Data and Declarative modes remain available for narrower integration choices.
Loaders read route data, actions perform route mutations, and pending navigation state supports feedback. Revalidation and cache policy determine when route data is fetched again.

Rendering strategy is selected per route and deployment target: client rendering, static prerender, server rendering, streaming, and partial prerendering each trade freshness, latency, infrastructure, and cacheability differently.
Choose a framework based on its routing model, server component maturity, runtime support, data and cache model, hosting constraints, ecosystem, and the team's operational requirements.

Future-flagged v8 behaviors became defaults, including always-on middleware and Vite environment API; minimum baseline moved to Node 22.22, React 19.2.7, and Vite 7; packages became ESM-only.
